name: Nōin-hōshi Amagoi no Kusunoki (Nōin's Rain-Praying Camphor)
species: Camphor Tree (Camphora officinarum, syn. Cinnamomum camphora)

location.address: Oyamazumi Shrine, 3327 Miyaura, Omishima-cho, Imabari City, Ehime Prefecture, Japan

verify_notes: BLOCKED, known dead. Ja.wikipedia states this camphor was already dead by 1941 and is now severely decayed with only a portion of its thick branches remaining ('太枝の一部だけが残る'). It is entry #26 of the nationally designated group 'Oyamazumi Shrine Camphor Tree Grove' (大山祝神社のクスノキ群, designated 1951-06-09), was historically the largest at the shrine (1941: 17m trunk circumference, 26m root circumference; by 1991 reduced to a 10m circumference, 10m tall remnant), and carries a real historical anecdote: in 1041 the monk Nōin performed a rain-prayer ritual here during drought, recorded in the Kinyō Wakashū (1127). Legendary age ~3,000 years, locally called 'Japan's oldest camphor', but the tree itself is gone. NOT the same tree as the already-published omi_001 'Ikiki no Gomon / The Living Gate' (34.24775, 133.00804, ~0.1km away): that is a separate, still-living camphor at the same shrine, explicitly identified in a further search as the largest LIVING camphor there ('生樹の御門', root circumference ~30m, evergreen, thriving). Do not confuse the two or attempt to 'revive' this entry by pointing it at the living tree; they are different trunks with different names. Hard rule: never publish a tree known to be dead as a collectible entry. No new leads file needed at the Omishima container since the city is already published; recording the block here so a future pass does not re-research this specific candidate.

name: Ono no Shidare-guri Jiseichi (Weeping Chestnut Natural Habitat of Ono)
species: Weeping Japanese Chestnut (Castanea crenata f. pendula, local name shidare-guri)

location.address: Ono, Tatsuno-machi, Kamiina-gun, Nagano Prefecture, Japan

verify_notes: BLOCKED as not a collectible point, same failure mode as the already-blocked Tado pear habitat. 'Jiseichi' confirms it in the name: this is a natural-growth HABITAT, designated a national Natural Monument on 1920-07-17, covering roughly 2.24 hectares of west-facing slope where 800-900+ weeping/pendulous chestnut trees grow as a naturally occurring mutant population (a spontaneous variant of Castanea crenata showing weeping branches and dying terminal buds, traditionally called 'tengu no kuri' after local folklore blaming tengu spirits for the trees' contorted shapes). It is one of only about five known sites of this variant in Japan and the largest. This is a population/area designation, not one named specimen and not a compact ensemble with one obvious place to stand (the Commons photo filenames themselves say 'Habitat... A/B/C', not a tree name), so it fails BRIEF_RESEARCH's single-collectible-point rule the same way an avenue or a whole wood does, regardless of the single-famous-tree destination exception (that exception is for one tree, not a forest population). Recommend recording as blocked in a Tatsuno-area leads file if one is ever created; no city currently published near this site (nearest published city per the brief is 36.2km away).

name: Shikishima no Kinmeichiku (Golden-Striped Bamboo of Shikishima)
species: NOT A TREE — Kinmeichiku bamboo, a variegated cultivar of Madake (Phyllostachys bambusoides f. castillonis); strictly the specimen is described as a form of Ginmeichiku

location.address: Kaminomori Hachiman-gu Shrine, 313-3 Tsukuda, Akagi-machi, Shibukawa City, Gunma Prefecture, Japan

verify_notes: BLOCKED, double failure. (1) Not a tree: kinmeichiku is a bamboo (a grass, Poaceae), out of this project's tree-only scope, whatever its designation status. (2) Not a collectible point even if scope allowed it: sources describe it as a '竹薪' (bamboo thicket/grove) of 100+ culms at Kaminomori Hachiman-gu shrine, designated a national Natural Monument 1953-11-14 — a population, not one specimen, the same failure as an avenue or a whole wood. Also flagging a CONTAINER ERROR in the brief: the address is Shibukawa City, Akagi-machi, Tsukuda 313-3, Gunma Prefecture — this is NOT in or near Numata; it does not belong on the Numata page under any distance reading, so it should not be filed as a Numata lead. No city currently published at Shibukawa. Note for the record: the grove nearly died after the bamboo's mass flowering (a natural die-back event for this species) in 1968 and was nursed back by the shrine's caretakers with pruning and fertilising, so even setting scope aside, its history is one of a managed population rather than a single ancient specimen.

name: Ushikubo no Nagi (The Nagi of Ushikubo)

location.address: Kumano Shrine, 87 Saidō-kaizu, Shimonagayama-cho, Toyokawa City, Aichi Prefecture, Japan

access: Free. Stands on the open grounds of a public Shinto shrine (Kumano Shrine), no gate or fee.
transport: JR Iida Line to Ushikubo Station, then about 6 to 10 minutes on foot (sources vary slightly, 6 and 10 minutes both cited).
verify_notes: DELIVERED AS A LEAD, not ready: verifies cleanly on facts but I judge it borderline on the 2026-08-31 single-famous-tree destination test and this is a judgement I'd rather a session or Hidde weigh in on rather than decide unilaterally either way. Facts are solid: a nationally designated Natural Monument since 1938-12-14 (online.bunka.go.jp, the official register), species confirmed as Nageia nagi by a geotagged 2013 Commons photograph whose EXIF coordinates (34°48'26.87"N, 137°22'48.34"E = 34.80746, 137.38010) match the candidate pin within a few metres, so location_precision is confirmed at tree level. Girth is given as 3.3m by the official Bunkacho record and 3.5m by the Toyokawa-area descriptive source (net-plaza.org); recorded girth_cm 340 as a rounded middle figure, note the 330-350cm spread rather than picking one. Height 20m and 'estimated over 300 years' both come only from the descriptive source, not the official register, so treated as a real-source vague estimate rather than sharpened. The tree is male (does not fruit), described alongside a separate female Nagi elsewhere in the same shrine grounds. Alive: no death or removal reported anywhere I found, described in the present tense by multiple town/shrine pages as a current sight ('現在...'), but the newest dated visual evidence I could pin down is the 2013 photograph (13 years old), so this is thinner than a 'last few years' confirmation and I flagged curation_status accordingly. On the destination test itself: it IS nationally designated, which is a real and fairly rare tier of protection, but at 45 views/month it sits at the bottom of this whole demand-ranked batch, sources describe it only as a regional/local sightseeing spot rather than a nationally famous pilgrimage tree, and it lacks the kind of standout legend or visual spectacle (a hollow shrine trunk, a destroyed Buddhist carving, a huge multi-stem clump) that made this batch's other 'own place' passes (e.g. Kawago no Okusu in an earlier batch) clear passes. Recommend a second opinion before publishing as a standalone page; all facts needed to write it are captured above if the answer is yes.
